ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *ǵnéw-der. Proto-Indo-European *ǵnéwom Proto-Germanic *knewą Proto-West Germanic *kneu Old English cnēo Middle English kne English knee Inherited from Middle English kne, from Old English cnēow, from Proto-West Germanic *kneu, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵnéw-o-m, a thematic derivative of *ǵónu.

senses.d: In humans, the joint or the region of the joint in the middle part of the leg between the thigh and the shank.
ex: Penny was wearing a miniskirt, so she skinned her exposed knees when she fell.
He made him ſtoup perforce vnto his knee, / And doe vnwilling worſhip to the Saint, / That on his ſhield depainted he did ſee[…]

senses.d: In the horse and allied animals, the carpal joint, corresponding to the wrist in humans.
The tarsal joint, uniting the tarsometatarsus and the tibiotarsus (homologous to the human ankle).
The joint uniting the tibiotarsus and the femur, typically hidden beneath plumage.
The part of a garment that covers the knee.
A piece of timber or metal formed with an angle somewhat in the shape of the human knee when bent.
An act of kneeling, especially to show respect or courtesy.
ex: Give them title, knee, and approbation.
[…] and he made a knee to the Caesar of Patna, giving that man all honour due to him.

senses.d: Any knee-shaped item or sharp angle in a line; an inflection point.
A blow made with the knee; a kneeing.
The presence of a parent etc., where a young child acquires early knowledge.
ex: The duty is, or should be, a thing taught at one's father's knee, and the structure of the family gently enforces it.
I could as well be brought / To knee his throne and, squire-like, pension beg / To keep base life afoot

senses.d: To poke or strike with the knee.
ex: When I blocked her from leaving, she kneed me in the groin.

senses.d: To move on the knees; to use the knees to move.
ex: Hassan kneed himself up, over, in, soundlessly, feet on floor, knife out, eyes like blunter knife trying to cut darkness.

grp.label: joint in the middle of the leg and area around it
carpal joint of a horse or related animal
To poke or strike with the knee

ety.text: Inherited from Old French genouz, genoilz plural of genoil, from Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu. Cognate with Bourguignon genô, Occitan genolh, Portuguese joelho.

Proto-Italic *rotā Latin rota Proto-Indo-European *-lós Proto-Indo-European *-elós Proto-Italic *-elos Latin -lus Latin -ellus Late Latin rotella Old Spanish rodiella Spanish rodilla Inherited from Old Spanish rodiella, from Late Latin rotella, diminutive of Latin rota (“wheel”).
Inherited from Old Spanish finojo, from Vulgar Latin *fenuclum, from Latin fēnuculum, from a diminutive of Latin fēnum.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese gẽolho, with metathesis, from Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu. Compare Galician xeonllo.
